analysis.one_liner: Adds a 10% tax on income above $2 million per year.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Don Beyer proposed an extra 10% tax on each dollar of income above $2 million (a $1 million threshold for single filers), on top of existing income taxes. The revenue would have gone to the federal treasury. The bill was sent to the tax-writing committee the day it was introduced and never moved again; it received no hearing, no vote, and expired when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the surtax would have raised revenue from a small number of very high-income households — those making over $2 million per household (over $1 million for single filers). All federal taxpayers benefit when a larger share of revenue comes from top earners instead of being raised elsewhere or added to deficits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal taxpayers, funded by top earners

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes an additional 10% tax on the portion of a household's adjusted gross income above $2 million, with the threshold dropping to $1 million for filers who do not file jointly.

The tax applies to individuals, estates, and trusts — not corporations — and reaches income from investments, not just wages, since it applies to all adjusted gross income with only a limited carve-out for investment interest deductions.

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 16,000 U.S. households with adjusted gross income above $2 million would pay the surtax. High-income filers with significant investment income that benefits from the investment interest deduction would also pay, since that deduction no longer reduces the tax base.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $2 million a year

drawbacks.text: Opponents of higher top rates argue that a surtax on very high earners can discourage investment, encourage income-shifting, and add complexity to the tax code, particularly for filers with income from businesses and investments.
The bill does not earmark the revenue for any specific purpose, so the burden on high earners is not tied to a concrete benefit voters could evaluate.

The bill never advanced, so it received no committee analysis, debate, or refinement — a tax change of this size would normally face scrutiny over design questions like thresholds that are not adjusted for inflation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy is a straightforward redistribution: a modest surtax on a very small group of the highest-income households, with essentially no direct cost to anyone else. Its main practical questions — economic effects on high earners, avoidance behavior, and what the revenue should fund — were never examined because the bill never got a hearing. As written, it is simple and targeted, though unvetted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Don Beyer of Virginia introduced the Millionaires Surtax Act on November 12, 2019, joined by six Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax legislation.
That was the bill's last action. The committee took no further steps, and the bill expired with the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning above $2 million per year are better off, since they avoid the 10% surtax. The Ways and Means Committee and House leadership are also unaffected in the sense that they never had to take a position, because the bill never reached a hearing or vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who avoid the surtax

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action; the bill never got a hearing or a vote.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Majority leadership that sets the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported it, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have added a 10% surtax on income above $2 million (or $1 million for single filers). Because the bill died, these households keep the status quo.

industries.industry: Wealth managers and tax planners serving high earners
industries.note: A new surtax on multimillion-dollar incomes would have created planning demand and complexity for tax professionals, but only if enacted.

The bill taxed adjusted gross income but disallowed the investment interest deduction from the surtax base, so highly leveraged investors would have owed more than under an ordinary income-based surtax. The bill never advanced, so the current rules stand.
